title: Communicative Competence — The Full Model

pts: Knowledge of vocabulary, grammar, phonology and spelling — the component Tier I's foundations focused on most directly.
Necessary but not sufficient on its own for effective real-world communication.
Overweighting this component alone is the most common trap in traditional language teaching.

v: Last three question papers; one coursebook unit

items: Collect the last three English question papers set for a class you teach.
Mark each question by the competence it mainly tests: grammatical (G), sociolinguistic (S), discourse (D) or strategic (St).
Calculate the percentage of marks for each.
Discuss what learners are likely to conclude about what ‘English’ means.
In a DIET or cluster meeting, groups audit papers from different districts and compare.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A typical pattern (written for this book):

lines: G: 60 per cent (grammar exercises, spelling, transformation). D: 25 per cent (a letter and a paragraph, but marked mainly for errors). S: 15 per cent (format of a formal letter). St: 0 per cent.

blocks.x: Grammatical competence (vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, spelling) remains essential. The trap is to treat it as the whole, so that learners who score well cannot use English outside the exam hall.

body: Purpose: to show grammatical competence as one of four parts. Content: a pie in four equal segments labelled with the four competences; beside it, a typical exam’s pie in which ‘Grammatical’ fills most of the circle. Style: clean infographic. Board version: two circles with pencil shading.

items: Google Sheets (free) for calculating percentages across papers.

blocks.x: A tally table in the teaching journal.

pts: The ability to use language appropriately for the social context — register, formality, politeness.
A grammatically correct utterance can still be sociolinguistically wrong for its situation.
This connects directly to Tier I's pragmatics work in Unit 24.

v: Eight utterance cards; four situation cards

items: Show a correct but inappropriate utterance: Give me leave tomorrow, said to the headmistress.
Ask: is it grammatical? Is it right for the situation? Why not?
Groups receive utterance and situation cards and match or mismatch them.
Groups rewrite each mismatch so that it fits its situation.
Discuss how the same request is made in learners’ home languages.
Learners collect real examples from notices, messages or films.
Support: a bank of polite forms (Could I…?, Would it be possible…?).
Challenge: explain which cue (relationship, setting, topic) made the utterance wrong.

blocks.x: Utterance and situation pairs (written for this book):

lines: Give me leave tomorrow. (to the headmistress) → Could I have leave tomorrow, please? My cousin is getting married.
I request you to kindly pass the salt. (to a brother at dinner) → Pass the salt, please.
Hey, what’s up? (opening a job application email) → Dear Ms Rao,
T: In Kannada, would you speak to the headmistress like that?
S1: No, we say ‘madam’, and use the respectful form.
T: Good. English shows respect differently, with ‘could’ and ‘please’, but the idea is the same.

blocks.x: Learners already have sociolinguistic competence in their home languages; English uses different means to the same end. This links to Unit 24 and prepares for politeness theory in Unit 53.

body: Purpose: to show that appropriateness depends on context. Content: a family kitchen and a headmistress’s office side by side, each with the speech bubble Give me leave tomorrow: a tick in the kitchen, a cross in the office. Style: friendly cartoon. Board version: two boxes and one sentence.

items: Wordwall (free basic plan) for a ‘match up’ activity with utterances and situations.

body: Canale and Swain’s original 1980 model had only three components. Discourse competence was separated from sociolinguistic competence a few years later, in Canale (1983), because connecting sentences into a text seemed to be a different kind of ability from choosing what is socially appropriate.

pts: The ability to produce and interpret coherent stretches of language, not just isolated correct sentences.
Cohesion devices — pronouns, connectors, ellipsis — are what make a sequence of sentences read as one connected text.
This is the competence genre-based writing work, later in this tier, builds most directly on.

v: A short paragraph cut into sentences, connectors removed

items: Give groups a paragraph cut into six sentences, with all connectors and most pronouns replaced by blanks.
Groups try to order the sentences and notice why it is hard.
Give them the missing words on slips; they complete and reorder.
Learners write a five-sentence paragraph on a similar topic, using at least three of the devices.
Use a short spoken anecdote transcribed from a colleague, with discourse markers removed.
Support: fewer sentences and a numbered first sentence.
Challenge: add an example of ellipsis or substitution (So did I, one).

blocks.x: A paragraph (written for this book), with the devices in bold:

lines: Mysuru is famous for its Dasara festival. It lasts ten days. During this time, the palace is lit with thousands of bulbs. However, the celebrations are not only for tourists. Many local families hold their own small ceremonies at home, and so do the schools.

blocks.x: Discourse competence is the ability to produce and interpret connected text. Cohesive devices (reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction and lexical links) signal how sentences relate (Halliday and Hasan 1976). Unit 33 develops genre and discourse; Unit 52 treats cohesion and coherence in depth.

body: Purpose: to show cohesion. Content: six sentence strips laid like bricks, with coloured mortar between them labelled it, however, during this time, so do. Style: simple, tactile. Board version: six rectangles with connecting words written in the gaps.

items: Google Docs (free) for preparing gapped and complete versions.

blocks.x: Sentence strips cut from a single sheet.

pts: The ability to compensate for gaps in knowledge — paraphrasing, circumlocution, asking for clarification.
Strategic competence is often what separates a fluent-seeming intermediate learner from a grammatically similar but less resourceful one.
This competence can be explicitly taught, not just left to develop by chance.

v: Picture cards of objects learners may not know the name of

items: Show a picture of an unusual object (a coconut scraper, a pressure cooker whistle) and pretend not to know its name.
Describe it aloud, and ask learners what you did.
Build a board list of strategy phrases (see model language).
In pairs, Learner A describes a card without naming it; Learner B guesses.
Swap and report which phrases helped most.
Learners describe objects from home for which they know only the home-language word.
Support: phrase frames on a card.
Challenge: a ‘banned words’ list for each card.

lines: It’s a kind of… / It’s something you use for… / It looks like… / I don’t know the word, but…
A: It’s a thing in the kitchen. You use it for coconut. It has a sharp round edge and you sit on it.
B: Ah, the coconut scraper! We have one at home.

blocks.x: Strategic competence is the ability to keep communication going despite gaps in knowledge (Canale and Swain 1980). It often explains why one intermediate learner seems fluent and another, with similar grammar, does not. Dörnyei and Thurrell (1991) argued that such strategies can and should be taught.

body: Purpose: to show strategic competence as a route around a gap. Content: a road with a gap labelled ‘missing word’ and a detour round it through ‘paraphrase’, ‘describe’, ‘ask’ and ‘gesture’ to ‘message understood’. Style: map-like, clear. Board version: a line with a gap and a curved arrow round it.

items: Quizlet (free basic plan) for picture cards of everyday objects.

blocks.x: Real objects brought from home, or hand-drawn cards.

pts: Present the same function (a request, a complaint) across several registers so learners see the range explicitly.
Authentic dialogue samples show register shifts better than invented, uniformly neutral textbook language.
Tie register choice to context cues learners can actually recognise — who's speaking, to whom, in what setting.

v: Five register cards; short dialogue transcripts

items: Choose one function, such as asking to borrow something.
Show five versions, from very informal to very formal, in random order.
Groups arrange them on a ladder from informal to formal.
Identify the language features that change (modals, please, names, length).
Groups write a short dialogue for a given relationship and setting; others guess who is speaking to whom.
Use complaints, apologies or invitations instead.
Support: three rungs instead of five.
Challenge: add a rung for a written email and compare it with speech.

blocks.x: A request ladder (written for this book):

lines: Pen? (to a close friend, pointing)
Can I borrow your pen?
Could I borrow your pen for a minute?
Would you mind if I borrowed your pen?
I wonder if I might borrow your pen for a moment.

blocks.x: Tie register to cues learners can recognize: who is speaking, to whom, where, and how big the favour is. Authentic dialogues show register shifts better than neutral textbook language. Remind learners that Indian English conventions (Respected Sir, kindly) are appropriate in some local settings and less expected in others.

body: Purpose: to show one function across registers. Content: a ladder with five rungs, each holding one version of the request; at the bottom two friends at a bench, at the top a learner speaking to a visiting official. Style: clean, warm. Board version: a ladder with five sentences.

items: YouGlish (free) for hearing phrases such as would you mind in real spoken English.

blocks.x: Teacher-performed dialogues with a colleague or a strong learner.

body: Ask learners how they would make the same request to a friend, an elder and an officer in their home language. Comparing markers of respect makes English register visible and values what learners already know.

pts: Explicitly teach connectors and cohesive devices as a distinct focus, not an incidental grammar point.
Learners often produce grammatically correct sentences that don't connect into a coherent paragraph without this focus.
This applies equally to spoken discourse markers (well, so, anyway) and written connectors (however, moreover).

v: A short spoken anecdote (live or recorded); a written paragraph

items: Tell a short anecdote, using natural spoken markers (well, so, anyway, actually).
Learners listen again and tick the markers they hear on a list.
Discuss what each marker does: starting, changing topic, returning, softening.
Contrast with written connectors in a short paragraph.
Pairs retell the anecdote, using at least three spoken markers.
Support: a marker card with functions in simple words.
Challenge: rewrite the spoken anecdote as a formal written paragraph.

lines: So, last Sunday we went to Lalbagh. Well, it was supposed to be a quiet walk, but actually there was a flower show. Anyway, we queued for an hour. And the best part? It rained.
Spoken: well (pausing, softening), so (starting, concluding), anyway (returning to the point), actually (correcting, contrasting).
Written: however (contrast), moreover (addition), therefore (result).

blocks.x: Without this focus, learners often write correct sentences that do not connect, or use formal connectors in casual speech (Moreover, I ate dosa).

body: Purpose: to contrast spoken and written markers. Content: two panels; on the left, two friends chatting with small signposts well, so, anyway above their speech; on the right, an essay page with signposts however, moreover, therefore in the margin. Style: light, two-colour. Board version: two columns of words.

items: BBC Learning English (free) for short audio and video with natural spoken language.

blocks.x: The teacher tells the anecdote live.

pts: Explicitly teach circumlocution, clarification requests, and paraphrase as usable strategies, not just hope learners find them.
Practice tasks that remove a key word deliberately force strategic competence into use.
This is one of the highest-value, lowest-cost additions a teacher can make to intermediate-level lessons.

items: Revise the strategy phrases from Point 4 and add clarification requests (Do you mean…?, Sorry, could you explain…?).
Groups of four: one learner describes a word on a card without saying it or the listed banned words.
The others guess, asking clarification questions.
Rotate describer every card; score one point per word guessed.
Groups share one strategy that worked.
Use words from the current coursebook or science chapter.
Support: fewer banned words; allow gesture.
Challenge: describe abstract words (freedom, patience).

lines: AUTO-RICKSHAW (banned words: three, wheels, driver, meter)
A: It’s a kind of vehicle. Yellow and black, usually. You take it for a short journey in the city.
B: Do you mean a taxi?
A: Similar, but smaller and open on the sides.

blocks.x: C: Auto! Removing a key word deliberately forces strategic competence into use. Explicit teaching of strategies is one of the highest-value, lowest-cost additions to intermediate lessons (Dörnyei 1995).

body: Purpose: to show the task format. Content: a card with a target word and four crossed-out banned words; three learners on a bench, one describing with her hands, two guessing. Style: playful. Board version: a rectangle with one word and four crossed words.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic plan) for a visible timer and random name picker.

blocks.x: Paper cards and the teacher’s watch.

pts: A speaking or writing rubric should score sociolinguistic and strategic competence explicitly, not just grammatical accuracy.
This previews the rubric-design work later in this tier (Unit 46), applied specifically to communicative competence.
Scoring only grammar quietly teaches learners that only grammar matters, regardless of what's said in class.

v: A current speaking or writing task; sample learner output

items: Take the rubric you currently use for a speaking or writing task.
Mark which criteria belong to which competence.
Rewrite it with four criteria, one per competence, each on a three-point scale.
Try it on two samples with a colleague and compare scores.
Share the rubric with learners before the next task.
Learners use a simplified version for self-assessment or peer assessment (Unit 43).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A four-criterion rubric for a two-minute role-play (written for this book):

lines: Grammar and vocabulary: 3 mostly accurate, good range / 2 some errors, meaning clear / 1 frequent errors block meaning.
Appropriateness: 3 register fits the situation / 2 mostly fits / 1 often wrong for the situation.
Organization: 3 ideas connected clearly / 2 some connection / 1 disconnected.
Strategies: 3 handles gaps and misunderstandings well / 2 sometimes / 1 stops when stuck.

blocks.x: Scoring only grammar quietly teaches learners that only grammar matters, whatever is said in class. Unit 46 develops rubric design for communicative performance in full.

body: Purpose: to show a balanced rubric. Content: a rubric grid with four coloured columns (matching Figure 27.1) and three rows of descriptors. Style: clear, printable. Board version: a four-by-three grid.

Vocaroo (free) for learners to record samples for later scoring.

body: Give your next speaking task two separate marks: one for grammar and vocabulary, and one for appropriateness and strategies. Tell learners in advance. Notice whether learners who usually stay silent attempt more when they know that getting round a gap earns credit.

dek: Unit 27 of 100: grammatical accuracy is only one quarter of what it takes to communicate well. This poster unpacks all four components and what teaching each one looks like.

aims.x: This unit develops the model of communicative competence introduced in Unit 26. It takes the four components one by one, shows what each looks like in a learner’s English, and then turns to practice: how to teach register, discourse markers and communication strategies, and how to assess all four components rather than grammar alone.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe the four components of communicative competence and how they interact;
explain why grammatical accuracy is necessary but not sufficient;
recognize sociolinguistic errors in utterances that are grammatically correct;
teach cohesive devices and discourse markers as a distinct focus;
teach communication strategies such as paraphrase and clarification requests explicitly;
present one language function across several registers;
design a rubric that rewards all four components.

why: Why this matters. A learner can be grammatically excellent and still communicate poorly. Naming the other three competences makes them teachable, not just noticeable when missing.

background.x: Dell Hymes (1972) coined the term communicative competence in reaction to Noam Chomsky’s narrower notion of linguistic competence. A speaker who could produce every grammatical sentence of a language, but had no idea when to speak or how to address an elder, would not be communicating well. Knowing a language, he argued, includes knowing how to use it appropriately in a community.

Michael Canale and Merrill Swain (1980) brought the idea into language teaching and testing. Their original model had three components: grammatical, sociolinguistic and strategic competence. Canale (1983) then separated out discourse competence, giving the four-part model that is still the most widely taught. Later models refined it (Bachman 1990; Celce-Murcia, Dörnyei and Thurrell 1995), and the CEFR Companion Volume describes linguistic, sociolinguistic and pragmatic competences separately (Council of Europe 2020).

For Indian classrooms the model has two implications. First, school English teaching and examining still concentrate on the grammatical component, because it is the easiest to exercise and mark. Second, appropriateness is not one universal standard: Indian English has its own conventions of politeness and address (Kachru 1983), and learners move daily between languages, each with its own norms. The NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 call for language use for real purposes and for multilingual approaches (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Teaching all four competences, and using learners’ knowledge of politeness in Kannada, Hindi or Tamil for comparison, fits both documents.

items: Competence profile. Record each learner’s rubric scores across a term and look for patterns by component.
Register task. Learners rewrite one request for three different listeners; assess appropriateness, not only accuracy.
Connected paragraph. Assess a short paragraph for cohesion as a separate criterion from grammar.
Strategy observation. Note which strategies each group uses in a describe-and-guess task.
What percentage of the marks in your question papers rewards each competence?
When did you last teach register explicitly rather than correct it in passing?
Which discourse markers do your learners overuse or never use?
What do your learners do when they do not know a word in English?
How can learners’ knowledge of politeness in their home languages help them with English?
Would your learners say that English class is about grammar, or about communication?

terms.def: A communication strategy in which a speaker who lacks a word describes or explains it instead, such as ‘the thing you use to open a bottle’.
The quality that makes a text make sense as a whole, with logically connected and relevant ideas; coherence depends on meaning, whereas cohesion depends on visible links.
The linking of sentences and ideas in a text through visible language devices such as pronouns, conjunctions, repetition and synonyms.
The knowledge and ability needed to use language appropriately in real situations, including grammar, social appropriacy, discourse and strategy, not only grammatical correctness (Hymes 1972).

The ability to combine sentences and utterances into coherent, cohesive spoken or written texts, for example by linking ideas and signalling the organization of a talk. It was added to the model of communicative competence by Canale (1983).
A word or phrase that organizes talk or writing and signals how ideas relate, such as so, anyway, well, however or on the other hand. Spoken markers are often missing from coursebook dialogues.
Knowledge of the vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation and spelling of a language, one component of communicative competence (Canale and Swain 1980).

Variation in language according to the situation of use, especially the subject matter, the relationship between participants and the channel of communication. A learner writes differently in a WhatsApp message to a friend and a leave letter to the headteacher.

Knowledge of how to use language appropriately in different social contexts, including politeness, register and social conventions (Canale and Swain 1980). Knowing how to address a principal as against a classmate is one example.
The ability to use verbal and non-verbal strategies to keep communication going when knowledge runs short, such as paraphrasing, asking for clarification or using gesture (Canale and Swain 1980).
